Female Longfin tilapia Oreochromis macrochir attain a maximum total length of 43 centimetres [Li = 43 centimetres], a value derived from extensive field surveys across the species' native range in south-central Africa. This ultimate body size places O. macrochir among the larger members of the genus Oreochromis, though it remains notably smaller than the Nile tilapia. The length-weight relationship for this species follows the allometric equation derived from a large specimen series, with the asymptotic body mass corresponding to approximately 1220 grams [Wwi = approximately 1220 grams]. This substantial adult mass reflects the species' ability to exploit productive floodplain habitats where food resources are seasonally abundant. The wet weight at birth is remarkably low, with newly hatched yolk-sac larvae weighing only 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter characteristic of many mouthbrooding cichlids. This tiny neonatal mass necessitates a brief but critical period of endogenous nutrition before the onset of exogenous feeding, during which the prolarva relies entirely on its yolk reserves while remaining sheltered within the buccal cavity of the attending parent.

At a stable water temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of Oreochromis macrochir has been documented through careful observation of captive breeding groups. Under these thermal conditions, gravid females produce approximately 4.1 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 4.1 eggs per day], a daily fecundity that accumulates into a substantial annual reproductive output. This high egg production rate, sustained over the extended breeding season, allows individual females to produce multiple clutches in succession, compensating for the relatively modest clutch sizes typical of mouthbrooding species. The thermal dependence of this reproductive trait is pronounced, as lower water temperatures substantially depress both the frequency of spawning events and the number of oocytes ovulated per cycle. Field observations confirm that the species initiates reproductive activity when water temperatures consistently exceed 24 °C, though the optimal thermal window for maximum fecundity clearly centres around the 30 °C [T = 30 °C] conditions under which these captive measurements were obtained.

The wet weight at puberty, estimated at 57.7 grams [Wwp = 57.7 grams], represents a substantial investment in somatic growth before reproductive allocation begins, a life-history strategy common among iteroparous cichlids that inhabit unpredictable floodplain environments. This puberty length is roughly one-third of the ultimate total length attained by females, indicating that O. macrochir delays reproduction until a relatively advanced stage of somatic development. The length-weight relationship used to derive this pubertal mass from the field-collected length data follows the same allometric equation applied to adult specimens, ensuring consistency across life stages. Captive-reared individuals typically reach this size and weight within six to nine months under optimal thermal and nutritional regimes, though wild populations exhibit considerably more variable growth rates depending on local conditions.

Longevity data for Oreochromis macrochir indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] when individuals are maintained at a constant water temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. This surprisingly long lifespan for a cichlid of moderate body size likely reflects the species' evolutionary history in stable, warm-water habitats where extrinsic mortality risks are relatively low. Senescent individuals in captivity typically exhibit a gradual decline in reproductive output during their final two to three years, with females producing progressively smaller clutches before ceasing spawning entirely. The natural mortality rate in wild populations is undoubtedly higher, with predation pressure from piscivorous birds and larger fish species representing the primary source of adult mortality. Nevertheless, the capacity for extended survival under favourable conditions allows O. macrochir to adopt a bet-hedging reproductive strategy, wherein reproductive effort is distributed across multiple breeding seasons rather than concentrated into a single, high-risk spawning event. This life-history pattern is consistent with that of other long-lived cichlids inhabiting seasonally productive freshwater ecosystems across the African continent.

The combination of a modest neonatal mass of 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams] and a substantial ultimate wet weight exceeding one kilogram (1220 grams) [Wwi = 1220 grams] defines a dramatic ontogenetic trajectory for Oreochromis macrochir, spanning five orders of magnitude in body mass. The total length at puberty of 15.6 centimetres [Lp = 15.6 centimetres] and the corresponding pubertal mass of 57.7 grams [Wwp = 57.7 grams] represent critical developmental benchmarks that govern the timing of reproductive onset. Under the thermal regime typical of this species' native range, with water temperatures averaging 30 °C [T = 30 °C] during the peak growing season, the maximum reproductive output of approximately 4.1 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 4.1 eggs per day] can be sustained for several consecutive months. The ultimate total length of 43 centimetres [Li = 43 centimetres] and the maximum documented lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years] together describe a species that invests heavily in somatic maintenance and reproductive longevity at a temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. These life-history parameters collectively position O. macrochir as a K-selected strategist relative to many other tilapiine cichlids, prioritising adult survival and repeated reproduction over rapid maturation and high fecundity, a strategy that has proven successful across the fluctuating floodplain environments of the upper Zambezi and Congo river basins.
